```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(error = FALSE)
old_options <- options("highcharter.theme")
```

## Choose a theme

Set a default at the top of a script to use the same theme for subsequent
charts. Widgets capture the theme when you create them. This example plots
monthly sales for the same two regions throughout the article.

```{r}
library(highcharter)

hc_set_theme("ft")

sales_chart <- function() {
  highchart(height = 260) |>
    hc_title(text = "Monthly sales") |>
    hc_xAxis(categories = c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun")) |>
    hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Units")) |>
    hc_add_series(name = "North", data = c(14, 17, 15, 21, 23, 24)) |>
    hc_add_series(name = "South", data = c(12, 14, 16, 17, 17, 20))
}

sales_chart()
```

To change a single chart, pass a theme to `highchart(theme = ...)` when
constructing it, or apply one to an existing widget.

```{r}
sales_chart() |> hc_add_theme(hc_theme("economist"))
```

## Create a theme in R

A theme accepts the same option names as Highcharts. Start from scratch or
override specific fields of a preset. For example, changing the colors below
preserves Carbon's typography, background and gridlines.

```{r}
team <- hc_theme(
  colors = c("#005F73", "#CA6702"),
  title = list(align = "left"),
  chart = list(backgroundColor = "transparent")
)

team_carbon <- hc_theme("carbon", colors = team$colors)
hc_set_theme(team_carbon)
sales_chart()
```

Use `hc_theme_merge(hc_theme("carbon"), team)` to reuse all of the options in
`team`. Nested fields merge by name. A supplied array replaces the previous
array, so a two-color palette stays two colors long.

## Inherit a Shiny app's theme

Use `hc_set_theme("bslib")` once at app startup. With Bootstrap 5.3, the
browser resolves the primary series color, base font, text, gridlines and
tooltip against the CSS around each chart. The transparent background lets
the card or page show through. Text and gridlines follow the page's color
mode. Other series use a categorical palette that you can replace with
`hc_colors()`. Chart titles use the base font.

```{r shiny, eval=FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(highcharter)

hc_set_theme("bslib")

ui <- page_fluid(
  theme = bs_theme(version = 5, primary = "#783356", base_font = "Georgia"),
  input_dark_mode(),
  highchartOutput("sales")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$sales <- renderHighchart(sales_chart())
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

If the project uses a `_brand.yml`, put the same choices there and use
`theme = bs_theme(version = 5, brand = TRUE)`. The chart takes the values that
bslib applies to the page. A standalone HTML widget uses the preset's
fallback colors and system font.

```yaml
color:
  primary: "#783356"
typography:
  base: Georgia
```

In a multi-user Shiny app, apply per-user choices with
`hc_add_theme(hc_theme(input$preset))` inside `renderHighchart()`.
The setter changes an R process option shared by its sessions.

## The collection

```{r}
hc_themes()
```

The FT adaptation uses its web paper color and categorical line palette.
Its separate bar palette applies to bars and columns with `colorByPoint = TRUE`.
For several bar series, pass `hc_theme("ft")$plotOptions$bar$colors` to
`hc_colors()`. The Economist adaptation uses dark and light blue as its first two series.
Carbon uses IBM's categorical sequence and blue sequential scale for maps
and heatmaps. The editorial presets are highcharter adaptations.
[FT chart colors](https://ft-interactive.github.io/g-chartcolour/) ·
[The Economist on chart colors](https://education.economist.com/blog/interviews/tips-for-visualising-data-like-the-economist) ·
[IBM Carbon palettes](https://carbondesignsystem.com/data-visualization/color-palettes/).

For a Carbon map of changes around zero, use a symmetric range and set the
neutral color at the midpoint. Reversing the signs would reverse the
interpretation of the two ends of this scale.

```{r}
change_theme <- hc_theme("carbon", colorAxis = list(
  min = -10, max = 10,
  stops = list(list(0, "#491D8B"), list(0.5, "#FFFFFF"), list(1, "#004144"))
))
```

Carbon draws gridlines in both directions and uses a circle wherever a series
displays a point marker. Tufte uses a gray palette, the Cardo font and small
y-axis ticks, leaving the plotting area open.

The remaining presets use the same sales data, except for the compact
single-series sparkline examples. The chalkboard, paper and sand textures
are embedded in the widgets and work offline.

```{r gallery, echo=FALSE}
other <- setdiff(hc_themes(), c("ft", "economist"))
htmltools::tagList(lapply(other, function(name) {
  chart <- if (name %in% c("sparkline", "sparkline_vb")) {
    highchart(height = 85) |> hc_add_series(data = c(14, 17, 15, 21, 23, 24))
  } else {
    sales_chart()
  }
  htmltools::tagList(htmltools::tags$h3(name), hc_add_theme(chart, hc_theme(name)))
}))
```

## Migrate an existing script

Replace `hc_theme_ft()` with `hc_theme("ft")`. A previous call to
`options(highcharter.theme = hc_theme_ft())` becomes `hc_set_theme("ft")`.
The collection contains 27 presets, including `db` (Dotabuff), `ffx`
(Firefox), `elementary` (elementary OS) and `google` (Google Books Ngram
Viewer). To reproduce the former `tufte2` style on a column chart, add an
x-axis baseline and draw white gridlines over the columns.

```{r}
bars <- hc_theme("tufte",
  xAxis = list(lineWidth = 1, lineColor = "#737373", tickWidth = 0),
  yAxis = list(lineWidth = 1, tickWidth = 0, gridLineColor = "white", gridZIndex = 4)
)
sales_chart() |> hc_chart(type = "column") |> hc_add_theme(bars)
```

```{r restore, include=FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
